title: Resident Retention Marketing for Apartment Communities: What Marketing Can Do for Renewals
seoDescription: What marketing can do for apartment renewals: resident updates, community content, review requests that follow Google and FTC rules, and what to measure.
excerpt: Marketing cannot fix slow maintenance or set renewal pricing, but it can make staying an easier decision for the residents you already have.
imageAlt: Two smiling young adults in burgundy jackets laughing together outside a blue front door, one holding a phone
imageIdea: Real photo of neighbors chatting outside an apartment entrance or at a community event, natural light, no brand logos.
author: The SocialDM Insights Team
bodyHtml:
Marketing cannot fix slow maintenance or a renewal increase well above the market, but it can make staying an easier decision. It does that by keeping residents informed, giving them reasons to know their neighbors, asking happy residents for reviews at the right moments, and making sure the renewal conversation starts early and reads clearly.

Most multifamily marketing budgets point at people who do not live at the community yet. Current residents get a welcome email, a few event flyers and a renewal letter. I think that is a mistake, because the people already living there are the audience you know best and the one whose reviews the next renter will read.

What can marketing actually do for renewals?

Marketing can shape how residents feel about the community over the whole lease, which is what they weigh when the renewal offer arrives. It cannot set the renewal price or fix operations, so it works best as a partner to the community manager, not a separate program.

In practice, marketing owns four things for residents: communication, community content, reviews and the renewal message itself. Operations owns service, pricing and policy. When those two groups plan together, residents hear one consistent story. When they do not, residents get a cheerful newsletter in the same week their work order sat open.

When should retention marketing start?

At move in, not at the renewal notice. The first few weeks set expectations about how the team communicates and responds, and every touch after that adds to or subtracts from the renewal decision.

Here is a simple timeline we use as a starting point. Adjust the renewal steps to your lease terms and local notice rules, which vary by state and city.

  • Move in week. A welcome message with how to submit work orders, where packages go, and who to call after hours.
  • About 30 days in. A short check in from the office asking how the move went. If the answer is good, this is a natural moment to ask for a review.
  • Ongoing. A monthly resident update, event invitations, and prompt notice of anything that affects daily life, such as water shutoffs or pool closures.
  • After a resolved work order. A quick follow up to confirm the fix held. A resident whose problem was solved fast is often the most willing to say so.
  • Before the renewal offer. A personal conversation or note from the community manager, so the offer is not the first message in months.
  • The renewal offer. Clear terms, clear options and a named person to talk to.

How should you ask residents for reviews?

Ask every resident who has a genuine experience to share, at moments when things have gone well, using Google's own review link or QR code. Never offer anything in exchange for a review, and never ask only the residents you expect to be positive.

Google's help page on creating a link or QR code to request reviews walks through how to get one from your Business Profile. Google's prohibited and restricted content policy says merchants may encourage reviews that reflect a genuine experience, but must not offer incentives, discourage negative reviews or selectively solicit positive ones. The FTC's rule on fake reviews and testimonials, announced in August 2024, separately bans offering incentives that are conditioned on a review being positive or negative, and bans certain tactics used to suppress negative reviews.

The safe pattern is simple: ask broadly, ask at good moments, and make it easy. Our Montage Tigard case study shows how we built that kind of playbook around happy moments for one community. When reviews come in, reply to them; our guide on how to respond to apartment reviews has examples.

What community content helps residents stay?

Content that makes the community feel known and cared for: useful updates, real events, and a sense of who the neighbors and nearby businesses are. The goal is that a resident would lose something they value by moving, not just a floor plan.

  • A resident update that is actually useful. Maintenance schedules, what changed and why, upcoming events, and one local feature such as a new restaurant nearby.
  • Events people want to attend. Smaller and more frequent often works better than one big party. Ask residents what they would come to.
  • Event recaps. Photos and short clips, with permission from anyone shown, posted to resident channels and, where appropriate, social media.
  • Local partnerships. Nearby businesses featured in resident content. Keep any perks unrelated to reviews.
  • Visible follow through. When residents ask for something and you deliver it, say so. "You asked for more package lockers, and they are in" builds trust better than any slogan.

Much of this content also works for prospects. A renter who sees a real event recap on your social channels learns more about the community than a stock photo can show.

What should you measure?

Measure retention marketing against renewals and resident sentiment, not opens and likes. The numbers below are the ones I would bring to an owner or asset manager.

MeasureWhy it matters
Renewal rate by monthThe outcome everything else supports
Reasons given on notices to vacateSeparates what marketing can influence from price, job moves and home purchases
Reviews from current residentsShows how residents describe the community in public
Themes in review textPoints to what to keep doing and what to fix
Event attendanceA rough read on whether residents feel connected
Work order follow up completionWhether the team closes the loop after a fix

Notice reasons matter most. If most residents leave to buy a home or relocate for work, better marketing will not change much. If they leave because they never felt connected, it can.

What should marketing avoid?

Do not promise in marketing what operations cannot deliver, and do not use residents' names, photos or stories without written permission. Do not tie any gift, raffle or perk to leaving a review, and do not route only happy residents to Google while sending everyone else to a private form.

Retention marketing also feeds your visibility. Reviews from long term residents, and the way residents describe the community, show up in Google Maps and in AI answers that renters read. That connection between residents and visibility is how we approach the work as a multifamily marketing agency.

Questions we hear

Can marketing really affect apartment renewals?

It can affect how residents feel over the whole lease, through communication, community content, reviews and a clear renewal message. It cannot fix pricing or slow service, so it works best alongside the community manager.

Can we offer residents a gift card or raffle entry for a Google review?

No. Google's policy prohibits incentives for reviews, and the FTC's 2024 rule bans incentives conditioned on a review being positive or negative. Ask broadly and make it easy instead.

Is it okay to ask only happy residents for reviews?

No. Google's policy says merchants must not selectively solicit positive reviews. Ask residents at good moments, but do not screen out the ones you expect to be critical.

When should we start talking to residents about renewal?

Retention starts at move in. Have a personal conversation before the formal offer arrives, and time the offer to your lease terms and local notice rules.

What is the most useful retention metric?

Renewal rate, read alongside the reasons residents give on notices to vacate. Those reasons show which move outs marketing could have influenced and which it could not.

sources.claim: Businesses can create a link or QR code from their Business Profile to request reviews
Merchants may solicit genuine reviews without incentives; must not offer incentives, discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive reviews

takeaways: Retention marketing starts at move in, not when the renewal offer goes out.
Ask every resident with a genuine experience for a review at good moments, using Google's review link or QR code.
Google prohibits review incentives and selectively asking happy customers, and the FTC's 2024 rule bans incentives tied to review sentiment.
Judge retention work by renewal rate and the reasons on notices to vacate, not by opens and likes.
